claims.text: The target eutectic high-entropy alloy has dual-phase lamellar colonies containing numerous internal boundaries.
Internal lamellar-colony boundaries serve as microcrack-initiation sites during room-temperature tensile loading.
A controlled heat treatment can nucleate coherent nanoscale precipitates at internal lamellar-colony boundaries.
Coherent nanoscale precipitates at colony boundaries enhance interfacial bonding.
The boundary precipitates act as crack deflectors or barriers.
The precipitates improve load transfer between alternating lamellar phases.
The precipitates delay microcrack initiation by relieving or redistributing interfacial stress concentrations.
The heat-treated eutectic high-entropy alloy will have higher room-temperature yield strength than the untreated lamellar baseline.
The heat-treated eutectic high-entropy alloy will have greater room-temperature uniform elongation than the untreated lamellar baseline.
The heat-treated alloy will show a delayed onset of microcracking during room-temperature tensile testing.
The untreated baseline has poorly bonded internal boundaries that cause tensile brittleness.
Simultaneous strength and ductility improvement requires a narrow processing window that produces uniformly distributed, coherent nanoprecipitates.
Heat-treatment parameters outside the proposed window may cause precipitate coarsening.
Heat-treatment parameters outside the proposed window may cause deleterious phase transformations.
The magnitude of the strength and ductility improvements depends on alloy composition and processing parameters.

contradictions.description: The boundary field limits the hypothesis to treatments that successfully form coherent nanoprecipitates within a narrow processing window, whereas the falsification rule treats failure to form those precipitates as falsification. Such a result could instead indicate an unsuccessful intervention or operation outside the stated boundary conditions.
